h1:
Sisaket Food Souvenirs
Pla Som, Naem, Shallots, Jasmine Rice & Durian Snacks
intro: Coming all the way to Sisaket and leaving empty-handed would be a shame, because this is a farming province with more to carry home than outsiders realise. There's pla som (fermented fish) and naem with that proper sour Isan tang, the GI shallots grown here more than anywhere else in Thailand, Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice, and volcanic durian snacks made from the province's GI durian. This guide walks you through what makes each edible souvenir special, which shop to buy it at, roughly how much it costs, and how to choose so you don't bring home a dud.

blocks.html: Sisaket isn't just Khmer ruins and the Pha Mo I Daeng cliff for sightseeing — it's a farming province where the good food really does come straight out of the ground: shallots grown here more than anywhere else in the country, jasmine rice from the Thung Kula Ronghai plains, and volcanic durian grown on basalt soil along the Phanom Dong Rak range. As a riverside Isan town, it also has fermented and pickled goods like pla som and naem that people have made here for generations. All of it works as a souvenir — you just need to know where to buy and how to pick.

blocks.text: What food souvenirs does Sisaket have?

blocks.html: Before we work through the shops, let's look at which edible souvenirs people most like to carry home from Sisaket. Each one keeps for a different length of time — some you need to eat fast, others ride a train across the next day no problem.

items: Pla som — sour-fermented freshwater fish, Isan style. Fry it or cook it into other dishes; the fresh kind needs refrigeration and should be eaten within a few days.
Naem / mam — sour-fermented pork, wrapped in banana leaf or in a casing. Eat it raw if it's properly fermented; a bit easier to carry home than pla som.
Shallots & garlic — the tied-bunch GI shallots and local garlic, the province's most famous product. Keeps for a month.
Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice — Khao Dawk Mali 105 white rice from the GI area, fragrant and soft, a souvenir everyone will happily eat.
Durian paste / volcanic durian snacks — durian paste, fried durian and dried durian made from GI volcanic durian. You can carry it home year-round, even out of season.
Pork floss, pork crisps, chilli pastes & kleeb lamduan cookies — dry souvenirs from the in-town souvenir shops, easy to keep and carry.

blocks.text: Pla som and naem — the fermented Isan goods locals gift

blocks.html: Pla som is freshwater fish fermented with roasted rice and salt until it turns sour — something Isan people have made forever. The Rasi Salai area and the Mun River basin within the province make a lot of it because the river supplies the fish. Fry pla som until crisp and eat it with steamed rice, or cook it into a chilli dip. Naem and mam are sour-fermented pork wrapped into bundles, eaten with ginger and fresh chillies. You'll find these at fresh markets in town and at dedicated pla som shops.

blocks.title: How to carry pla som and naem home without it spoiling
blocks.html: These fermented goods are perishable. Tell the vendor how many hours you'll be travelling and they'll vacuum-pack them or pack them with ice · over half a day, keep a cooler in the car · refrigerate the moment you get home, and always fry pla som until fully cooked before eating.

blocks.text: Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice — the souvenir everyone eats

blocks.html: Thung Kula Ronghai is a vast plain straddling five Isan provinces, and Sisaket holds part of it around the Rasi Salai and Sila Lat districts. The rice grown here is Khao Dawk Mali 105 and RD 15, grown once a year as wet-season rice, with a natural fragrance that earned it a GI registration as Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice. It makes a great souvenir because anyone can eat it, it keeps a long time, and you can buy it vacuum-packed to carry onto a plane or train easily. Go for new rice early in the season — that's when it's most fragrant and soft.

blocks.text: Durian paste and volcanic durian snacks — carry them home all year

blocks.html: Sisaket volcanic durian is a GI durian grown on basalt soil weathered from ancient volcanoes around Kantharalak, Khun Han and Si Rattana. Fresh durian season runs roughly June to August only, but if you come out of season or want something that keeps, the processed goods are the answer: chewy, rich-sweet durian paste, crispy fried durian, dried durian and durian ice cream. These are made from local durian, easy to carry home and far longer-keeping than fresh fruit — perfect for anyone who wants to try the volcanic durian flavour without having to come in season.

blocks.title: Check the border situation first
blocks.html: The volcanic durian orchards and sights like Pha Mo I Daeng–Khao Phra Wihan sit along the Kantharalak border. Border conditions can change. If you plan to drive up to buy durian at the orchards or stop at the viewpoints, check the border situation and whether the area is open before you set off, every time. If you just want the souvenirs, buying in town gets you the same goods.

blocks.text: Where to buy food souvenirs — the shops locals go to

blocks.html: Sisaket's souvenirs are spread across several spots: long-running souvenir shops in town, shops gathering the best goods of the four Tai ethnic groups, fresh markets, durian orchards and online sellers. Below are the places people actually go, laid out by what each one does best. Prices are rough ranges that depend on the season and the type of product.

items.name: Kit Tiang (near the train station)
items.blurb: A long-running souvenir shop open over 60 years on Khukhan Road, near Sisaket train station. They make and pack everything themselves — pork floss, pork crisps, pork sheets, rice crackers, chilli pastes, shallot cookies and kleeb lamduan cookies. Ideal if you've just got off the train and want to grab dry goods straight away — one stop covers a lot.
items.meta: Khukhan Rd, near the train station · dry souvenirs
items.price: Dry goods/sweets from tens to hundreds of THB

items.name: Sisaket Souvenir Shop, Mae Si Roundabout
items.blurb: A souvenir shop in the city centre around the Mae Si Sa Kes roundabout, with lots of options in one place: pickled solo garlic, homemade bakery, kleeb lamduan cookies, shallot cookies, local fabrics and handicrafts. Good for anyone who wants several souvenirs sorted in a single shop — easy to find, easy to park.
items.meta: Mae Si Roundabout, city centre · mixed souvenirs
items.price: Sweets/processed goods from a few hundred THB

items.name: Mae Si Mart (Sao Ang sweets, 4 Tai groups)
items.blurb: A souvenir shop showcasing the good goods of Sisaket's four Tai ethnic groups, with local sweets like khanom sao ang, shallot-and-garlic processed goods and woven crafts. Good for anyone after souvenirs with a real local cultural flavour rather than generic stuff.
items.meta: In Sisaket city · local goods of 4 Tai groups
items.price: Local sweets from tens to hundreds of THB

items.name: Ban Khanom Rakhang Thong
items.blurb: An in-town souvenir shop known for sweets and homemade bakery, with kleeb lamduan cookies (the provincial sweet), cookies and dry desserts that carry home easily. Good for anyone who wants sweet-tooth souvenirs to hand out at the office or to the family.
items.price: Sweets from tens to hundreds of THB

items.name: Sisaket Municipal Fresh Market
items.blurb: An in-town fresh market where you can find the full range of fresh souvenirs: pla som, naem, mam, shallots, garlic and local fermented-pickled goods. Market prices are cheaper than the souvenir shops — good for anyone after genuine Isan fermented goods from vendors who make it themselves. Ask them to pack it spoil-proof.
items.price: Pla som/naem by weight, market price

items.name: Pla som & fermented-goods shops, Rasi Salai area
items.blurb: Rasi Salai sits in the Mun River basin and the Thung Kula Ronghai plains — an area that makes a lot of pla som and fermented goods because the river supplies the fish. Drive through here and you'll find stalls and shops selling their own pla som, fresh from the source. Good for anyone travelling the Rasi Salai–Roi Et route.
items.meta: Rasi Salai district · pla som heartland
items.price: Pla som sold by the kilo, source price

items.name: Volcanic durian orchards & shops (Kantharalak/Khun Han)
items.blurb: From June to August, drive up around Kantharalak, Khun Han and Si Rattana, where orchards and shops sell volcanic durian both as fresh fruit and as processed goods like durian paste and fried durian. Good for anyone who wants goods straight from the orchard — but check the season and the border situation first, since it's near the border.
items.price: Durian paste/processed from a few hundred THB

items.name: Wholesale shallot-garlic market, Talat Tha Ruea area
items.blurb: An in-town wholesale market for shallots and garlic, where the traders buy their stock. Goods are fresh and cheapest because they come straight from the growing areas. Good for anyone after bunch-tied shallots or lots of garlic by the sack to split up and give away. It gets very busy during harvest season.

items.name: Provincial OTOP / community enterprise shops
items.blurb: Processed goods made and sold by the province's farmer groups: fried shallots, pickled garlic, shallot cookies, vacuum-packed jasmine rice, even durian paste. Find them at OTOP shops and provincial fairs. Good for anyone after community-made goods you won't find elsewhere.
items.price: From a few hundred THB depending on type

items.name: Online shops from local farmers
items.blurb: If you can't make it to Sisaket, many local farmer groups and shops sell on Shopee, Lazada and Facebook pages — GI jasmine rice, bunch-tied shallots and durian paste. Pick a seller that states the growing area clearly, has reviews and lists a production date, so you get goods close to buying it yourself.

blocks.title: Which goods suit whom
blocks.html: Want dry goods to carry straight onto the train? Head to Kit Tiang · want several things sorted in one shop? Go to Mae Si Roundabout · want fresh pla som and naem? Go to the municipal fresh market · want durian paste straight from the orchard? Drive up to Kantharalak in season · want lots of cheap shallots? Go to the wholesale market.

blocks.text: A 2-day souvenir-shopping trip — buy it all without missing anything

blocks.html: If you're in Sisaket and want to gather a full haul of both fresh and dry souvenirs, here's a short plan to follow — adjust it depending on whether you've come during durian season.

items.activity: Get off the train, stop at Kit Tiang near the station
items.note: Grab pork floss, pork crisps, kleeb lamduan cookies and shallot cookies — dry goods you can carry straight away

items.activity: Head to Mae Si Roundabout — the mixed souvenir shop + Mae Si Mart
items.note: Pick up pickled garlic, the four Tai groups' local sweets and vacuum-packed jasmine rice

items.activity: Stop by the wholesale market in the Talat Tha Ruea area
items.note: Bunch-tied GI shallots and garlic, cheaper than the souvenir shops — buy plenty to split up

items.activity: Walk the in-town evening market, sample some food before buying fresh goods
items.note: Scout pla som and naem prices to come back and buy the next day before leaving

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Fresh & fermented goods, before heading home

items.note: Pick up pla som, naem, mam and fresh fermented goods — ask the vendor to pack them spoil-proof for the long trip

items.activity: In season (Jun–Aug), drive up to Kantharalak for volcanic durian
items.note: Buy durian paste/fried durian straight from the orchard — always check the border situation first

items.activity: Out of durian season, buy processed durian paste in town instead
items.note: OTOP shops or mixed souvenir shops have ready-packed durian paste to carry home

items.activity: Run through your fresh/dry checklist, pack your bags before boarding
items.note: Fresh goods in a cooler, dry goods straight into your carry-on

blocks.text: How to choose food souvenirs without getting it wrong

blocks.html: Edible souvenirs include fresh goods where you check freshness and processed goods where you check the production date. If you're buying a lot to give to several households, run through these to be safe.

items: Pla som & naem — it should smell sour and fragrant, not rotten; the flesh firm, not mushy. Ask the fermentation date and have it packed spoil-proof.
Shallots & garlic — pick firm bulbs with dry skins, deep red colour and small necks; they'll keep longer without going mouldy.
Jasmine rice — choose new rice early in the season with long, clean grains, and look for the Thung Kula Ronghai mark or GI label if you want the real thing.
Durian paste & fried durian — check the production and expiry dates and that it's sealed tight; durian paste should be smooth in texture, not hard.
Sweets & dry goods — check the production date and the FDA (อย.) number, especially if you're buying a lot to give away.

blocks.title: How to get it all home intact
blocks.html: Keep fresh and dry goods in separate bags · put fresh items like pla som and naem in a cooler and refrigerate the moment you get home · don't seal bunch-tied shallots in an airtight bag — let them breathe · rice and durian paste can go in your carry-on, but check the airline's rules on liquids and strong-smelling items first.

faq.q: What are Sisaket's most famous food souvenirs?
faq.a: The ones people most like to carry home are the bunch-tied GI shallots and garlic, Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice, durian paste and processed snacks made from GI volcanic durian, plus Isan fermented goods like pla som and naem, and dry goods such as pork floss, pork crisps and kleeb lamduan cookies from the in-town souvenir shops.

faq.q: Where's the best place to buy Sisaket souvenirs all in one stop?
faq.a: In town there's Kit Tiang near the train station and the mixed souvenir shop around Mae Si Roundabout — both have plenty of dry and processed goods sorted in a single shop. For fresh goods like pla som and naem, go to the municipal fresh market; for lots of cheap shallots, go to the wholesale market in the Talat Tha Ruea area.

faq.q: Can pla som and naem be carried home over long distances?
faq.a: Yes, but they're perishable and need care. Tell the vendor how many hours you'll be travelling and they'll vacuum-pack them or pack them with ice. Over half a day, keep a cooler in the car; refrigerate the moment you get home; and always fry pla som until fully cooked before eating.

faq.q: Can I still buy volcanic durian souvenirs out of season?
faq.a: Yes. Fresh durian is only around June to August, but processed goods like durian paste, fried durian and dried durian are sold year-round at souvenir shops and OTOP shops in town. They're easy to carry home and keep far longer than fresh fruit.

faq.q: How is Sisaket's Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice different from ordinary rice?
faq.a: It's Khao Dawk Mali 105 and RD 15, grown as wet-season rice in the Thung Kula Ronghai area around Rasi Salai and Sila Lat. The natural fragrance from the local soil and water earned it a GI registration. Choose new rice early in the season for the most fragrant, softest grains.
